'''Martin A. Lindquist''' is a statistician and biostatistician whose work focuses on functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), neuroimaging methodology, brain connectivity, causal inference, and pain neuroscience. He is a professor in the Department of Biostatistics<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://publichealth.jhu.edu/departments/biostatistics|title=Biostatistics &#124; Johns Hopkins &#124; Bloomberg School of Public Health|website=publichealth.jhu.edu}}</ref> at the [[Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health]]. His research has included statistical modeling of the hemodynamic response in fMRI, dynamic functional connectivity, mediation analysis in neuroimaging, and methodological work on reliability, preprocessing, and biomarkers in brain imaging.

== Early life and education ==

Lindquist was born in [[Stockholm]], [[Sweden]]. He completed an MSc in engineering physics at the [[KTH Royal Institute of Technology|Royal Institute of Technology]] (KTH) in Stockholm in 1997 and earned a PhD in statistics from [[Rutgers University]] in 2001. His doctoral dissertation was titled ''Fast Functional MRI Using Two-Dimensional Prolate Spheroidal Wavefunctions''. His thesis advisors were [[Lawrence Shepp]] and Cun-Hui Zhang.

== Career ==

After completing his doctorate, Lindquist was a postdoctoral associate at the Center for Magnetic Resonance Research at the [[University of Minnesota]] from 2001 to 2002. He joined [[Columbia University]] in 2002 as an assistant professor of statistics and became an associate professor in 2008. In 2012 he moved to [[Johns Hopkins University]] as an associate professor of biostatistics, and in 2015 he became a full professor.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://sites.google.com/view/martinlindquist/home|title=Home|website=sites.google.com}}</ref>

== Research ==
Lindquist's published work spans several areas of neuroimaging statistics. His early research included methods for rapid fMRI acquisition and the statistical analysis of high-temporal-resolution imaging data.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Rapid three-dimensional functional magnetic resonance imaging of the initial negative BOLD response |journal=Journal of Magnetic Resonance |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1090780707003710}}</ref> He later published on hemodynamic response modeling,<ref>{{cite journal |title=Modeling the hemodynamic response function in fMRI: Efficiency, bias and mis-modeling |journal=Human Brain Mapping |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1053811908012056}}</ref>  dynamic functional connectivity,<ref name="auto2">{{cite journal |title=Evaluating dynamic bivariate correlations in resting-state fMRI: A comparison study and a new approach |journal=NeuroImage |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1053811914005291}}</ref> and reliability in neuroimaging research.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Neuroimaging results altered by varying analysis pipelines |journal=Nature |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-020-01282-z}}</ref> He has also published on causal inference and mediation analysis for neuroimaging data, including functional causal mediation<ref name="auto">{{cite journal |title=Functional Causal Mediation Analysis With an Application to Brain Connectivity |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.2012.695640}}</ref> and high-dimensional mediation models.<ref>{{cite journal |title=High-dimensional multivariate mediation with application to neuroimaging data |journal=Biostatistics |url=https://academic.oup.com/biostatistics/article/19/2/121/3868977?guestAccessKey=}}</ref> His more recent work has addressed pain neuroimaging<ref>{{cite news |title=Before Pain Turns Chronic |url=https://magazine.publichealth.jhu.edu/2023/pain-turns-chronic |work=Hopkins Bloomberg Public Health Magazine}}</ref> and neuroimaging-based biomarkers.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Building better biomarkers: brain models in translational neuroimaging |journal=Nature Neuroscience |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/nn.4478}}</ref> His co-authored publications include work on neurologic signatures of physical pain.<ref name="auto1">{{cite journal |title=An fMRI-Based Neurologic Signature of Physical Pain |journal=New England Journal of Medicine |url=https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1204471}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Big Data Analytics of Brain Scans May Pinpoint Biomarkers |url=https://magazine.publichealth.jhu.edu/2018/big-data-analytics-brain-scans-may-pinpoint-biomarkers |work=Hopkins Bloomberg Public Health Magazine}}</ref> He is a principal investigator on the Acute to Chronic Pain Signatures (A2CPS) project, which seeks to identify biomarkers and advance the study of pain.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://prod.a2cps.tacc.utexas.edu/directory/|title=Directory|website=prod.a2cps.tacc.utexas.edu}}</ref>

Lindquist also developed online courses, including ''Principles of fMRI I'', ''Principles of fMRI II'', and ''The Statistical Analysis of fMRI Data'', offered through [[Coursera]], which have reached 100,000 students world-wide.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.coursera.org/learn/functional-mri|title=Principles of fMRI 1|website=Coursera}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.coursera.org/learn/functional-mri-2|title=Principles of fMRI 2|website=Coursera}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/author/martin-a-lindquist-7307/|title=MIT Press}}</ref>

Together with [[Tor Wager]], he co-authored Principles of fMRI,<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://leanpub.com/principlesoffmri|title=Principles of fMRI|first1=Tor D.|last1=Wager|first2=Martin A.|last2=Lindquist|date=December 20, 2025|via=leanpub.com}}</ref> a low-cost book on fMRI data analysis.

== Honors and awards ==
Lindquist was elected a [[Fellow of the American Statistical Association]] in 2016.<ref>{{Cite web |title=ASA Fellows |url=https://ww2.amstat.org/fellows/ |access-date=September 1, 2026 |website=American Statistical Association}}</ref> In 2018 he received the Organization for Human Brain Mapping Education in Neuroimaging Award.<ref name="auto3"/>

== Selected works ==
* Lindquist, Martin (2008). "The Statistical Analysis of fMRI Data". ''Statistical Science''.<ref>{{cite journal |title=The Statistical Analysis of fMRI Data |journal=Statistical Science |url=https://projecteuclid.org/journals/statistical-science/volume-23/issue-4/The-Statistical-Analysis-of-fMRI-Data/10.1214/09-STS282.full}}</ref>
* Lindquist, Martin (2012). "Functional Causal Mediation Analysis with an Application to Brain Connectivity". ''Journal of the American Statistical Association''.<ref name="auto"/>
* Wager, Tor; Atlas, Lauren; Lindquist, Martin; Roy, Mathieu; Woo, Choong-Wan; Kross, Ethan (2013). "An fMRI-based Neurologic Signature of Physical Pain". ''New England Journal of Medicine''.<ref name="auto1"/>
* Lindquist, Martin; Xu, Yuting; Nebel, Mary Beth; Caffo, Brian (2014). "Evaluating Dynamic Bivariate Correlations in Resting-state fMRI: A comparison study and a new approach". ''NeuroImage''.<ref name="auto2"/>
* Lindquist, Martin; Geuter, Stephan; Wager, Tor; Caffo, Brian (2019). "Modular Preprocessing Pipelines can Reintroduce Artifacts into fMRI Data". ''Human Brain Mapping''.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Modular preprocessing pipelines can reintroduce artifacts into fMRI data |journal=Human Brain Mapping |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/hbm.24528}}</ref>
